extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and NaNoWriMo participants (writers attempting a 50,000-word November draft)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing a first-draft novel of ~50,000 words during National Novel Writing Month (November), following NaNoWriMo community practices and constraints. Emphasizes rapid drafting, daily word targets, and post-November revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: 50,000-word target / daily word count
rubrics_metrics.description: Write 50,000 words in November (1,667 words/day average). 50K is the loose minimum for a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formal challenge is to reach 50K by the end of November; treat 1,667 words/day as the average target to stay on track. This is a pragmatic production goal rather than a guarantee of a polished novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't Edit While You Write
rubrics_metrics.description: "NaNoWriMo's golden rule." The month is for getting story onto page; revision comes later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premature editing kills momentum; prioritize forward progress and completion of a discovery/first draft during November. Save structural and line-level edits for post-November revision periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach: Plotter vs. Pantser
rubrics_metrics.description:
- Plotter — outlines extensively before writing
- Pantser — "writes by the seat of their pants"; discovery-drafts
- Most writers are somewhere between
- NaNoWriMo accommodates both styles
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a method that lets you hit the daily target: plotters should use outlines to accelerate drafting; pantsers should accept exploration and discovery. Hybrid approaches are common and acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily Word Count Discipline / Showing Up
rubrics_metrics.description: The work happens through showing up. 1,667 words/day is achievable; consistency beats inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize routine and discipline over waiting for inspiration. Treat the month as a production sprint where consistent daily writing is the primary success factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan Ahead (for Plotters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline structure; brief cast of characters; research locations; have premise + ending in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plotters are advised to prepare scaffolding (structure, character notes, research) before November to maximize drafting speed. Having a premise and an intended ending helps avoid mid-month drift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower Initial Quality Bar
rubrics_metrics.description: First drafts are supposed to be rough. Lamott's "shitty first drafts" applied at industrial scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that quality will be low during the sprint; the goal is raw material to revise later. Trying to produce polished prose during the challenge is an anti-pattern that undermines completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community Accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Public word counts, regional groups, write-ins. Social pressure helps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use NaNoWriMo community features (tracking, local write-ins, forums) to maintain momentum and accountability. Peer support can substitute for intrinsic motivation during the sprint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected deliverable: first draft, not a polished novel
rubrics_metrics.description: A polished story is rarely produced by NaNoWriMo alone — but a first draft is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the November output as a draft that typically requires substantial subsequent revision. Do not evaluate NaNo output by polished-novel standards; instead evaluate by completion and usable raw material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common structural problems in NaNoWriMo novels
rubrics_metrics.description: 50K novels written in 30 days have characteristic structural problems: rushed endings, undercooked middles, voice inconsistencies, plot contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware these recurring failure modes when drafting and plan fixes during revision (e.g., pacing work on middles, consistency passes for voice and plot threads). For modeling or critique, these patterns are diagnostic of sprint-produced drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implications for quality modeling and corpus use
rubrics_metrics.description: NaNoWriMo-style writing is a key training and reference corpus for understanding amateur fiction. The community's own discussions about what works/doesn't form a folk craft taxonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using NaNoWriMo corpora for analysis or ML, account for systematic biases of rapid-drafting (structural weaknesses, roughness). Leverage community-generated taxonomies and discussions as domain knowledge for labeling or feature design.
